comment: Brian (ElevenLabs) VO for the WorldCup26.world MILESTONE + FIFA-RECORDS documentary (~24 min, target 1470s). Channel milestone: 14,000 subscribers (owner-stated). Every fact VERIFIED + sourced (hard rule #9); WC2026 has been played so results are stated as fact (real-results rule). SOURCES: Final Spain 1-0 Argentina a.e.t. 19 Jul 2026, Ferran Torres 106', Emi Martinez 11 saves (final record), Enzo Fernandez sent off, Spain 2nd title & first nation to hold men's+women's cups at once [CBS; ESPN espn.com/soccer/story/_/id/49403084; Yahoo]. Awards: Rodri Golden Ball, Messi Silver, Mbappe Bronze + Golden Boot 10 goals (first to win it twice) [NBC Sports; Irish Times; FIFA]. Messi tourney: 8 goals, 4 assists, 5 POTM [Sports Mole; Khel Now]; IFFHS named Messi best player, contradicting FIFA [IFFHS iffhs.com]. All-time scorers: Klose held 16 (2002-2014), SURPASSED at WC2026 - Mbappe 22, Messi 21 [ESPN espn.com/soccer/story/_/id/49140402]. PRIZE MONEY 2026 [FIFA inside.fifa.com council release; Al Jazeera]: total pool $655M (+50% vs 2022); winner (Spain) $50M record; runner-up (Argentina) $33M; 3rd $29M; every team guaranteed $10.5M ($9M minimum prize + $1.5M preparation) [SI; CNBC cnbc.com/2026/07/19]. CLUB BENEFITS $355M to clubs (~$11,000/player/day at the finals, $250M finals pot + $100M for qualifying-release clubs (~$2,362/player/match, first time ever) — up ~70% from $209M in 2022) [FIFA inside.fifa.com landmark-club-benefits; Bolavip] [FIFA; Reuters]. Money growth [topendsports]: 1982 ~$2M, 2006 ~$20M, 2018 $38M, 2022 $42M, 2026 $50M. Records: Brazil 5 titles & only ever-present nation [Britannica]; youngest scorer Pele 17y239d 1958; oldest Roger Milla 42 (1994); fastest goal Hakan Sukur 10.8s 2002 [FIFA]. WC2026: first 48-team/104-match, 3 hosts, 39 days; 308 goals (highest-scoring ever); attendance 6,810,966 (avg 65,490); Spain conceded 1 goal in 8 games [Sportmonks; Olympics.com; ESPN]. Greatest winners: Brazil 1970 (won all 6; Jairzinho scored every match), Spain 2010 tiki-taka, Brazil 1958/62 [SI; Britannica]. Greatest-never-won: Cruyff/Netherlands 1974, Puskas/Hungary 1950s, Roger Milla [Bleacher Report]. Trump-Balogun: Balogun red-carded vs Bosnia (R32); Trump phoned Infantino; ban suspended under Article 27; ALSO little-known: Ronaldo's qualifying red card (vs Ireland) was likewise suspended so he could play Portugal's opener [fotmob; CBS]; the unverified 'first since 1962' claim was CUT (rule #9); UEFA said FIFA 'crossed a red line'; USA still lost Belgium 4-1 [Wikipedia 2026 Trump-FIFA red card controversy; PBS/AP; Al Jazeera; CNBC]. NO on-screen sentence text - labels/number-cards only. App CTA: free, just for fun, no prizes. Avoided flagged errors: Klose stated historically; NO 'biggest final win' claim; used official $50M winner figure.

lines.text: On a July night, in a packed stadium outside New York, the whole world held its breath.
A substitute. Extra time. One touch... and it was over.
Spain — champions of the world. Argentina, a fingertip away. And Lionel Messi, walking off with everything... except the trophy.
The greatest tournament ever staged had just ended.
Forty-eight nations. One hundred and four matches. More than six and a half million people in the stands.
Tonight, we're not previewing a game. Tonight we ask a bigger question.
What does a World Cup leave behind — the money, the records, the legends? And what did we build, together, while it happened?
Welcome back to WorldCup twenty-six. This one is special.
So let's rewind.
Not long ago, this was just an idea. A stubborn little belief — that the World Cup belongs to the fans. So the fans should get to play it, not only watch it.
And so we built worldcup twenty-six dot world.
The rule is simple. You pick three of the forty-eight nations. And every goal they score... scores for you.
Free to play. Just for fun. No prizes — only pride, bragging rights, and a climb up the leaderboard.
Then came the Legend Cards.
A collection of football's immortals — each one telling you the story they never told... in a voice I think you've come to know.
We made cinematic episodes. The match myths. The previews. The forgotten heroes history tried to erase.
And the Shorts — sixty-second stories nobody else was brave enough to tell.
The one-armed man who scored in the very first World Cup final... and won it.
The gentleman of football, who paid the ultimate price for an own goal.
The boy who became a goalkeeper... just to escape his own father.
Real stories. Verified, never invented. Soccer, always — clean enough for anyone, deep enough to move you.
And with every episode, we raised the bar. Better animation. Better sound. Deeper research.
No broadcaster. No rights deals. No stolen highlights. Just original art, honest history, and a game you can actually play.
That was the whole mission. And somewhere along the way...
something incredible happened.
You turned a handful of subscribers... into fourteen thousand.
Fourteen thousand.
Say it slowly. Because it deserves it.
A year ago, our entire audience could have squeezed into a living room.
Today? You would fill a football ground. A whole roaring end of a stadium — and that is you.
Fourteen thousand people who chose these stories. Who chose the legends over the noise.
Every like. Every comment. Every time you sent a Short to the friend who swore Messi was finished — you built this.
We read every comment. We see the same names, again and again. You've become a team.
And we do not — not for one second — take you for granted.
So from the bottom of our hearts... thank you.
But here's the thing about a milestone. It is not a finish line.
It's base camp.
The tournament is over. The stories never are. And we are only just getting started.
So let's celebrate the only way we know how. With a story. Actually — with all of them.
The money. The records. The greatest of all time. And the moments this World Cup will never be allowed to forget.
Let's begin with the number that stops everyone cold.
Money.
Because twenty twenty-six wasn't just the biggest World Cup ever. It was the richest single month in the history of sport.
FIFA put a record six hundred and fifty-five million dollars on the table.
Fifty percent more than four years ago. In one cycle.
The champions, Spain, took home fifty million dollars. One cheque. For lifting one trophy.
The most any team has ever been paid to win the World Cup.
Argentina, beaten in the final, still earned thirty-three million. Third place, twenty-nine.
And no nation went home empty-handed. Simply qualifying guaranteed every team ten and a half million dollars... before a single ball was kicked.
But here's the part almost nobody talks about. The clubs.
FIFA paid three hundred and fifty-five million dollars — to the clubs who released their players.
Roughly eleven thousand dollars, per player, for every single day he was at the tournament.
That quiet squad player at the back of your team's bench? If he was here... your club got paid, every day he stayed.
A record for the clubs too — up almost seventy percent in four years.
And it was not always like this. Not even close.
In nineteen eighty-two, the world champions earned around two million dollars. Two.
By two thousand and six — twenty million.
Twenty eighteen — thirty-eight. Twenty twenty-two — forty-two.
And now — fifty.
The winner's cheque has grown roughly twenty-five times over... inside a single lifetime.
The trophy hasn't changed. The stakes have exploded.
One good World Cup can now fund an entire football nation for years.
That's the money. Staggering. But money was never why we fell in love with this game.
We fell in love with the records. And the men who broke them.
So — who owns the record books?
Start with the kings. Brazil. Five stars on the shirt.
Fifty-eight. Sixty-two. Seventy. Ninety-four. Two thousand and two.
And the only nation to appear at every World Cup ever held. Every single one.
Then, the scorers. For twelve years, one name ruled — Miroslav Klose, of Germany. Sixteen World Cup goals. They called it untouchable.
And then came this summer.
Two men tore that record to pieces.
Kylian Mbappé. And Lionel Messi.
Both flew past Klose. Mbappé finishing his World Cup story on twenty-two goals. Messi, on twenty-one.
A record that had stood for over a decade — broken twice, in the same tournament.
Mbappé took the Golden Boot with ten goals — the first man in history to win it twice.
The youngest ever to score at a World Cup? Pelé. Seventeen years old. Nineteen fifty-eight.
The oldest? Roger Milla, of Cameroon. Forty-two years young — dancing at the corner flag, in nineteen ninety-four.
The fastest goal in World Cup history still belongs to Hakan Şükür. Ten point eight seconds. Blink — and it's in.
But twenty twenty-six didn't just join the record books. It rewrote the biggest pages of all.
The first ever forty-eight-team World Cup. One hundred and four matches. Three host nations. Thirty-nine days.
Three hundred and eight goals — the highest-scoring men's World Cup ever played.
Nearly six point eight million fans through the gates.
An average of sixty-five thousand a game — stadiums filled almost to the last seat, night after night.
And the champions themselves set a record of quiet steel.
Spain conceded exactly one goal. In eight matches. The meanest defence any World Cup winner has ever had.
Numbers, on numbers, on numbers. But numbers alone never made anyone cry.
Greatness does.
So which winners were the greatest of them all?
Ask a hundred historians, and most begin in the same place.
Brazil. Nineteen seventy.
Six matches. Six wins. Pelé, Jairzinho, Carlos Alberto — football played like a dream.
Jairzinho scored in every single game of that tournament. No one has ever done it again.
Then Spain, two thousand and ten. Tiki-taka.
Xavi and Iniesta, passing opponents into dizziness — a team that didn't beat you. It hypnotised you.
The back-to-back Brazilians of fifty-eight and sixty-two, who unwrapped a teenage Pelé for the world.
West Germany's relentless machine. Italy's cool artists of eighty-two.
Each one — a completely different way to be perfect.
And now, Spain, twenty twenty-six, force their way into that conversation.
Because this Spain did something no country in history had ever done.
They held the men's and the women's World Cups... at the very same time.
Champions of both. The first nation ever. Let that sink in.
Different eras. Different colours. Different styles.
But every great champion shares one thing. They made the whole world stop, and watch.
And yet...
here is the strangest truth in all of football.
Some of the most loved names of all... never lifted the cup at all.
Because the World Cup is not only remembered for who won.
It's remembered for how it made us feel.
Think of Johan Cruyff — the Dutch genius of nineteen seventy-four, who reinvented how football is played... and lost the final.
Or Ferenc Puskás, and the magical Hungarians of the fifties — the greatest team many say never lifted it.
Or Roger Milla, who never won a thing — but gave the world a dance nobody has stopped copying.
No trophies. And yet we still say their names, all these years later.
And this summer... we watched it happen again. In real time.
Lionel Messi. His sixth World Cup. The one he said would be his last.
Eight goals. Four assists. Five times the best man on the field.
At thirty-nine years old, he dragged Argentina all the way to the final kick of the tournament.
And then, Spain. Rodri, choking the midfield. Argentina reduced to ten men.
Emi Martínez making eleven saves in the final — a record — holding on with his fingertips.
And then the substitute. Ferran Torres. The hundred and sixth minute. One-nil.
It was enough. It was over.
Messi walked off with a runner-up medal. And then came the cruellest twist of all.
Even the Golden Ball — the award for the best player of the tournament — went to Rodri.
Messi was given the Silver.
The greatest of all time. His final World Cup. No trophy. No golden ball.
And yet.
Ask anyone who was in those stands what they will remember.
They won't tell you the score. They'll tell you they saw Messi.
One global football body even overruled FIFA — and named him the player of the tournament anyway.
Because some prizes cannot be handed out on a stage.
The love of millions is one of them.
He didn't win the cup. He won something that doesn't fit inside a trophy case. And he always will.
And then there was the moment... that had nothing to do with football at all.
The United States. Playing at home. Their striker, Folarin Balogun, sent off against Bosnia, in the round of thirty-two.
An automatic ban. He'd miss the next match. The rules are the rules.
Except — the President of the United States picked up the phone.
Donald Trump called the head of FIFA, and asked him to look at the card again.
And FIFA did. They reached for a rule buried deep in their code... and suspended the ban. Balogun was free to play.
And almost nobody noticed — Cristiano Ronaldo arrived here the same way. A qualifying red card... suspended, so the legend could play his opening night.
Europe's football body said FIFA had crossed a red line. The game was furious.
And the ending history will never forget?
With their striker back on the pitch... the United States lost to Belgium. Four to one.
Some things... not even a president can fix.
That... is what a World Cup leaves behind.
The richest prizes in sport — and the man who won none of them, loved the most.
Records that stood for decades, gone in one summer. A goal in extra time that crowned a nation. And a phone call that shook the game.
Glory. Heartbreak. Controversy. Joy. All of it — in thirty-nine unforgettable days.
And us? Fourteen thousand strong. And climbing.
Here's our promise for what comes next. More legends. More records. More of the stories nobody else will tell you.
So if you're new here — subscribe. You're early. The best is still ahead.
And come play with us. At worldcup twenty-six dot world, pick your three nations. Every goal — yours.
Free. Just for fun. No prizes — only glory.
Collect the legends. Learn the stories they never told you. And we'll see you... in the next one.
Thank you. For everything.
